**LLN says averages settle; CLT describes the shape of their remaining fluctuations under additional conditions.** These are related but different statements. The law of large numbers concerns convergence toward an expectation. The classical IID central limit theorem concerns the distribution of a centered, properly scaled average when variance is finite. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

**A coin illustration.** As more fair-coin flips are averaged, the head fraction tends toward one half. That is the LLN intuition. Across many repeated experiments of N flips, the distribution of the fraction around one half becomes approximately Gaussian after scaling by its standard error. That is the CLT intuition.

The CLT does not say the original observations become normal, nor that every sample size of 30 is automatically sufficient. Tail behavior, skew, and dependence affect approximation quality.

**Heavy tails separate the theorems.** Cauchy observations do not have a finite mean or variance; their average remains Cauchy rather than concentrating in the usual way. Some Pareto distributions have a finite mean but infinite variance, allowing an LLN while the classical finite-variance normal CLT fails. Other limiting laws or normalizations may apply.

Before using standard errors, examine the data-generating process, clustering, serial dependence, and outliers. More rows do not create more independent information if observations are strongly related. State which version of a limit theorem and which assumptions justify the approximation used in an analysis.

**Technical details and references.**

The law of large numbers concerns convergence of the sample average to the expectation under suitable assumptions. The classical iid CLT states that finite-variance averages, after centering and scaling, converge in distribution to a normal law. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

$$\sqrt N\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma}\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,1).$$

LLN does not say the finite-sample error is Gaussian or provide its rate. A Cauchy distribution has no finite mean/variance; averaging iid Cauchy observations remains Cauchy, so this CLT does not apply. Some Pareto distributions have finite mean but infinite variance: an LLN can hold while the classical normal CLT fails. Dependence also requires additional conditions. Diagnose tail behavior and dependence before using standard-error formulas or treating observations as independent.
